source_text: EVANGELICA praecepta, fratres dilectissimi, nihil aliud sunt quam magisteria divina, fundamenta aedificandae spei, firmamenta corroborandae fidei, nutrimenta fovendi cordis, gubernacula dirigendi itineris, praesidia obtinendae salutis; quae, dum dociles credentium mentes in terris instruunt, ad coelestia regna perducunt. Multa et per Prophetas servos suos dici Deus voluit et audiri; sed quanto majora quae Filius loquitur, quae Dei sermo qui in Prophetis fuit propria voce testatur, non jam mandans ut paretur venienti via, sed ipse veniens, et viam nobis aperiens et ostendens; ut qui, in tenebris mortis errantes, improvidi et caeci prius fuimus, luce gratiae luminati, iter vitae duce et rectore Domino teneremus. Qui inter caetera salutaria sua monita et praecepta divina quibus populo suo consulit ad salutem, etiam orandi ipse formam dedit, ipse quid precaremur monuit et instruxit. Qui fecit vivere, docuit et orare, benignitate ea scilicet qua et caetera dare et conferre dignatus est; ut, dum prece et oratione quam Filius docuit apud Patrem loquimur, facilius audiamur. Jam praedixerat horam venire quando veri adoratores adorarent Patrem in spiritu et veritate, et implevit quod ante promisit; ut qui spiritum et veritatem de ejus sanctificatione percepimus, de traditione quoque ejus vere et spiritaliter adoremus. Quae enim potest esse magis spiritalis oratio quam quae a Christo nobis data est, a quo nobis et Spiritus sanctus missus est? Quae vera magis apud Patrem precatio quam quae a Filio, qui est Veritas, de ejus ore prolata est? ut aliter orare quam docuit non ignorantia sola sit, sed et culpa, quando ipse posuerit et dixerit: Rejicitis mandatum Dei, ut traditionem vestram statuatis. Oremus itaque, fratres dilectissimi, sicut magister Deus docuit. Amica et familiaris oratio est Deum de suo rogare, ad aures ejus ascendere Christi oratione. Agnoscat Pater Filii sui verba cum precem facimus. Qui habitat intus in pectore, ipse sit et in voce. Et cum ipsum habeamus apud Patrem advocatum pro peccatis nostris, quando peccatores pro delictis nostris petimus, advocati nostri verba promamus. Nam, cum dicat quia quodcumque petierimus a Patre in nomine ejus dabit nobis,, quanto efficacius impetramus quod petimus in Christi nomine, si petamus ipsius oratione? Sit autem orantibus sermo et precatio cum disciplina, quietem continens et pudorem. Cogitemus nos sub conspectu Dei stare. Placendum est divinis oculis et habitu corporis et modo vocis. Nam, ut impudentis est clamoribus strepere, ita contra congruit verecundo modestis precibus orare. Denique magisterio suo Dominus secreto orare nos praecepit, in abditis et semotis locis, in cubiculis ipsis, quod magis convenit fidei; ut sciamus Deum ubique esse praesentem, audire omnes et videre, et majestatis suae plenitudine in abdita quoque et occulta penetrare, sicut scriptum est: Ego Deus approximans, et non Deus de longinquo. Si absconditus fuerit homo in absconditis, ego ergo non videbo eum? Nonne coelum et terram ego impleo? Et iterum: In omni loco oculi Dei speculantur bonos et malos. Et quando in unum cum fratribus convenimus, et sacrificia divina cum Dei sacerdote celebramus, verecundiae et disciplinae memores esse debemus, non passim ventilare preces nostras inconditis vocibus, nec petitionem commendandam modeste Deo tumultuosa loquacitate jactare, quia Deus non vocis sed cordis auditor est. Nec admonendus est clamoribus qui cogitationes hominum videt, probante Domino et dicente: Quid cogitatis nequam in cordibus vestris? Et alio loco: Et scient omnes ecclesiae quia ego sum scrutator renis et cordis.
pass_a_gloss: The evangelical precepts, most beloved brothers, are nothing other than divine teachings, foundations for building hope, reinforcements for strengthening faith, nourishments for fostering the heart, guiding principles for directing our journey, and defenses for obtaining salvation; which, while instructing the teachable minds of believers on earth, lead them to the heavenly kingdoms. God wanted to be called and heard by many through the prophets, His servants; but how much greater are the things that the Son speaks, which the Word of God, who was in the prophets, testifies with His own voice, no longer commanding that a way be prepared for Him who is coming, but Himself coming and opening and showing us the way; so that we, who previously wandered in the darkness of death, unwise and blind, might, illuminated by the light of grace, hold to the path of life with the Lord as our guide and director. Among other health-giving admonitions and divine precepts by which He consults for the salvation of His people, He Himself also gave the form of prayer, and instructed and warned us what we should pray for. He who made us live also taught us to pray, with that kindness by which He deigned to give and confer other things upon us; so that, while we speak to the Father with the prayer and supplication that the Son taught, we may be more easily heard. He had already foretold that the hour would come when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, and He fulfilled what He had promised beforehand; so that we, who have perceived the spirit and truth from His sanctification, may also worship truly and spiritually from His tradition. For what prayer can be more spiritual than the one given to us by Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit was also sent to us? What prayer can be more true before the Father than the one spoken by the Son, who is the Truth, from His own mouth? So that to pray otherwise than He taught is not only ignorance, but also guilt, when He Himself said and established: You reject the commandment of God, that you may establish your own tradition. Let us pray, therefore, most beloved brothers, as God, our teacher, taught. It is a friendly and familiar prayer to ask God for what is His, to ascend to His ears with the prayer of Christ. Let the Father recognize the words of His Son when we make our prayer. He who dwells within our breast should also be in our voice. And when we have Him as our advocate with the Father for our sins, when we, sinners, ask for forgiveness for our offenses, let us pronounce the words of our advocate. For, when He says that whatever we ask of the Father in His name, He will give us, how much more effectively do we obtain what we ask for in the name of Christ, if we ask with His own prayer? However, let our speech and prayer be with discipline, containing quiet and modesty. Let us consider that we stand before the eyes of God. We must please the divine eyes with both the posture of our body and the manner of our voice. For, just as it is shameless to cry out with clamors, so it is fitting to pray with modest and reverent prayers. Finally, by His own teaching, the Lord commanded us to pray in secret, in hidden and remote places, in our own chambers, which is more fitting for faith; so that we may know that God is present everywhere, hears all, and sees all, and with the fullness of His majesty penetrates even into hidden and secret places, as it is written: I am a God who approaches, and not a God from afar. If a man hides in hidden places, shall I not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? And again: The eyes of God watch over the good and the evil in every place. And when we come together with our brothers, and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of God, we ought to be mindful of modesty and discipline, not to scatter our prayers everywhere with uncontrolled voices, nor to commend our petition to God with tumultuous loquacity, because God is the hearer not of the voice, but of the heart. Nor does He need to be reminded with clamors, who sees the thoughts of men, as the Lord approves and says: Why do you think evil in your hearts? And in another place: And all the churches will know that I am the examiner of kidneys and heart.

pass_b_english: The evangelical precepts, dearest brothers, are nothing other than divine teachings: they lay the foundations for building hope, reinforce faith, nourish the heart, guide our journey, and defend the salvation we obtain. While they instruct the teachable minds of believers on earth, they lead us to the heavenly kingdoms. God willed to be proclaimed and heard many times and in many ways through his servants the prophets, but how much greater are the words the Son speaks. The Word of God, who was in the prophets, now testifies with his own voice. He no longer commands that a way be prepared for the one who is coming; instead, he himself comes, opening and showing us the way. We once wandered in the darkness of death, unwise and blind. Now, illuminated by the light of grace, we hold to the path of life with the Lord as our guide and director.

Among his other salutary admonitions and divine precepts by which he provides for his people's salvation, he himself gave us the form of prayer, instructing and warning us what we should ask. He who gave us life also taught us to pray, out of the same kindness by which he deigned to grant all his other gifts. He did this so that, when we speak to the Father with the prayer and supplication the Son taught, we may be more easily heard. He had already foretold that the hour was coming when true worshipers would worship the Father in spirit and truth, and he fulfilled what he had promised. Because we have received the Spirit and truth from his sanctification, we must also worship truly and spiritually through his tradition. What prayer could be more spiritual than the one given to us by Christ, from whom the Holy Spirit was also sent to us? What prayer could be more true before the Father than the one spoken from the mouth of the Son, who is the Truth? To pray otherwise than he taught is therefore not only ignorance but also guilt, since he himself said: 'You reject the commandment of God, that you may establish your own tradition.'

Let us pray, then, dearest brothers, as God our teacher taught. It is a friendly and familiar prayer to ask God for what is his own, lifting his words to the Father's ears on the wings of Christ's prayer. Let the Father recognize the words of his Son when we make our petition. The one who dwells within our breast should also be in our voice. Since we have him as our advocate with the Father for our sins, when we sinners ask forgiveness for our offenses, let us pronounce the words of our advocate. He said that whatever we ask of the Father in his name he will give us. How much more effectively, then, do we obtain what we seek in Christ's name if we ask with his own prayer?

Yet our speech and prayer must be marked by discipline, preserving quiet and modesty. Let us remember that we stand before the eyes of God. We must please the divine gaze with both our bodily posture and our manner of voice. It is shameless to cry out with clamor; it is fitting, rather, to pray with modest, reverent prayers. Finally, by his own teaching the Lord commanded us to pray in secret, in hidden and remote places, in our very chambers. This befits faith, so that we may know God is present everywhere, hears all, and sees all, and that the fullness of his majesty penetrates even into hidden and secret places. As it is written: 'Am I a God at hand, declares the Lord, and not a God far away? Can a man hide himself in secret places so that I cannot see him? declares the Lord. Do I not fill heaven and earth?' (Jer 23:23-24). And again: 'The eyes of the Lord are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good' (Prov 15:3).

And when we gather together with our brothers and celebrate the divine sacrifices with the priest of God, we must be mindful of modesty and discipline. We must not scatter our prayers with uncontrolled voices, nor commend our petition to God with tumultuous loquacity, for God is the hearer not of the voice but of the heart. He does not need to be reminded by clamor, since he sees the thoughts of men. The Lord approves and says: 'Why do you think evil in your hearts?' (Matt 9:4). And in another place: 'All the churches will know that I am he who searches mind and heart' (Rev 2:23).

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass A provides a faithful clause-by-clause translation, and Pass B provides a fluent English rendering that preserves all theological distinctions and causal relations. Scripture citations added in Pass B (Jer 23:23-24, Prov 15:3, Matt 9:4, Rev 2:23) correctly identify the biblical allusions present in the Latin text (Ego Deus approximans...; In omni loco oculi Dei...; Quid cogitatis...; scrutator renis et cordis).

The Latin text is accurately translated in the Pass A and Pass B versions. The title 'The Lord's Prayer' correctly reflects the content of the passage. The translation preserves the original meaning, including the theological concepts, structure, and citations. The scripture citations match the quoted or alluded-to content. No errors or omissions are found in the translation.
